A dromedary is a type of camel — specifically, the camel with one hump on its back. Its scientific name is Camelus dromedarius. That single hump is the most important detail: it is what sets the dromedary apart from the Bactrian camel, which has two humps. A handy memory trick — the letter D (as in Dromedary), when turned on its side, looks like one hump. The letter B (as in Bactrian) looks like two humps.

A dromedary is a large animal — roughly 1.8 to 2 metres tall at the shoulder and weighing between 400 and 600 kg. It has long legs, a long neck, a relatively lean body, and a coat that is typically sandy beige or brown, though it can range from nearly white to dark brown.

Its feet are wide and flat with two toes, which spread out on sand the way snowshoes spread weight on snow — this stops the animal from sinking into the ground as it walks across deserts.

It has thick, bushy eyebrows, double rows of long eyelashes, and nostrils that can seal shut. These are not decoration — they protect the dromedary's eyes and airways during sandstorms.
The hump: what is it really?

Many people believe the hump stores water. This is a very common myth. The hump actually stores fat — a concentrated reserve of energy that the dromedary draws upon when food is scarce. It can hold up to about 36 kg of fat.

When a dromedary is well-fed, its hump stands firm and upright. When it has gone without food for a long time, the hump shrinks, softens, and may even flop to one side. Once the animal eats and rests well, the hump fills back up.

Dromedaries are native to the Arabian Peninsula and the Horn of Africa (the northeastern tip of Africa — countries like Somalia and Ethiopia). Over thousands of years, humans spread them across North Africa, the Middle East, and parts of Central Asia.

There is also a large population in Australia — descendants of domesticated dromedaries that were brought over in the 19th century and later released or escaped. These feral dromedaries now number in the hundreds of thousands and are considered a serious pest because they damage native vegetation and water sources.

True wild dromedaries no longer exist. Every dromedary alive today is either domesticated or feral.
How are dromedaries built for desert life?

The dromedary is one of the most remarkably adapted animals on Earth when it comes to surviving in hot, dry, harsh environments. Here is how:

Water management:
Dromedaries can survive for weeks without drinking water if they are eating moisture-rich plants. In intense heat with no water at all, they can go about a week. When they do finally reach water, they can drink an astonishing 100 to 200 litres in a single session lasting just 10 to 15 minutes.

Their body handles water loss very differently from most mammals. Their urine is extremely concentrated, and their dung is very dry — both of which mean they lose very little water in waste. Their red blood cells are oval-shaped rather than round (most mammals have round ones). This matters because when a dromedary is severely dehydrated, its blood thickens. Oval cells can still move through thick blood; round cells would clog up.

Temperature tolerance:
A dromedary's body temperature is not fixed the way a human's is. It can rise from about 34°C in the cool of night to about 41°C in the heat of the day — a range of 7 degrees — without the animal becoming ill. This means it doesn't need to start sweating until it's very hot, which saves a huge amount of water.

Eating in the desert:
The dromedary has thick, tough lips that allow it to eat thorny, spiny desert plants that would injure most other animals. It is essentially unbothered by vegetation that would cut through softer mouths.

Dromedaries were domesticated roughly 3,000 to 4,000 years ago, most likely on the Arabian Peninsula. They quickly became indispensable to desert-dwelling peoples and have served humans in many ways:

  • Transport: They can carry loads of 150 to 200 kg across long distances through terrain that is impassable to wheeled vehicles. They were, and still are, called "ships of the desert" for this reason.
  • Riding: Humans ride dromedaries both for travel and in racing events.
  • Milk: Camel milk is highly nutritious and rich in vitamins. In many communities across Africa and the Middle East, it is a dietary staple.
  • Meat: Dromedary meat is consumed in several parts of the world.
  • Wool and hides: Their coarse hair is used to make textiles and rope, and their skin is used for leather.
Dromedary vs. Bactrian camel: a quick comparison

Since the two are often confused, it helps to have this clearly in mind:

  • Dromedary → 1 hump → native to hot desert regions (Arabia, Africa)
  • Bactrian camel → 2 humps → native to cold, rugged terrain in Central Asia (like the Gobi Desert)

The Bactrian camel is stockier and has a shaggier coat suited to cold climates. The dromedary is taller and leaner, built for heat.

There are about 14 to 15 million dromedaries in the world, making them far more numerous than Bactrian camels.
How the word is used in sentences

• "The caravan crossed the Sahara on a line of dromedaries."
  • "She photographed a dromedary at the wildlife reserve, noting how its single hump distinguished it from the two-humped camels she had seen at the zoo."
  • "Dromedaries were essential to trade routes across the Arabian Desert for thousands of years."

A dromedary is the one-humped camel — a large, desert-adapted mammal domesticated for thousands of years and used for transport, milk, and meat. Its hump stores fat (not water), and its body is engineered with extraordinary precision to survive heat and dehydration. It is native to Arabia and Africa, though today it is found across the broader arid world — and unexpectedly, in very large feral numbers in the Australian outback.
